name: Francisco de Herrera the Elder
teaser: The fierce Seville painter who may have taught Velázquez — his dramatic, dark works with violent brushwork made him one of the founders of the Spanish Baroque. His temper was so notorious that his own son fled to study elsewhere.

exploreAction.targetName: The Triumph of St. Hermenegild or the Vision scenes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the energy: Herrera painted with a rough, loaded brush long before Velázquez or Zurbarán smoothed things out. His saints burst with movement and shadow. He was difficult, brilliant, and self-taught in the hardest way. Velázquez may have learned his boldness here.

name: Juan Bautista Maíno
teaser: The Spanish painter who fused Caravaggio's realism with Venetian color — his Adoration of the Shepherds is a dark, tender masterpiece of tenebrism. He later became a Dominican friar and taught the young prince who would become Philip IV.

exploreAction.targetName: The Adoration of the Shepherds (Prado) — the light
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the darkness: Maíno lit his Nativity with a single source — the child himself — so the whole scene glows from the manger. The shepherds' faces are real, sunburned, amazed. He took Caravaggio's drama and gave it a Spanish warmth.

name: Vicente Carducho
teaser: The Italian-born painter who became the theorist of Spanish Baroque painting — his frescoes in the Carthusian monastery of El Paular are among the most ambitious cycles of the century, and his dialogues on painting defended the artist's dignity.

exploreAction.targetName: The El Paular Carthusian cycle — the scenes
exploreAction.instruction: Fifty-four large paintings of the Carthusian order's history fill the monastery's cloisters. Look at how Carducho stages each scene with theatrical clarity — his monks suffer, pray, and die in painted light. He also wrote that painting was a noble art, not a craft — a bold argument in 1633.

name: Antonio de Pereda
teaser: The Spanish painter of vanitas and still life — his allegories of earthly vanity pile skulls, globes, coins, and playing cards into dark, sumptuous warnings. His still lifes are among the finest in Spanish art.

exploreAction.targetName: The Knight's Dream or the vanitas paintings
exploreAction.instruction: Look at The Knight's Dream: a young man sleeps while an angel offers a choice — heaven above, a table of pleasures and a skull below. Every object is a symbol: the coins, the cards, the armor. Pereda painted luxury's cost, and made the warning gorgeous.

name: Antonio Palomino
teaser: The Spanish painter who wrote the book — his Lives of the Eminent Spanish Painters and Sculptors (1724) is the reason we know anything about Velázquez, Zurbarán, and Murillo. His own frescoes and portraits are skilled, and his biography of the art world is priceless.

exploreAction.targetName: The frescoes in the parish of St. John the Baptist, Madrid — the illusion
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how Palomino painted the cupola: saints and angels float in painted sky, spilling over the frame — classic Baroque illusion, done late and well. Then open his book: it's a gossipy, reverent history of the Golden Age, written by someone who knew everyone in it.

name: Alonso Cano
teaser: The Spanish painter, sculptor, and architect nicknamed 'the Spanish Michelangelo' — a man of three arts and a violent temper (he was suspected in his wife's murder, then acquitted). His Immaculate Conception in Granada is serene beyond belief.

exploreAction.targetName: The Immaculate Conception (Granada Cathedral) — the calm
exploreAction.instruction: The Virgin floats on a crescent moon among wheat, lilies, and a host of putti — painted with a sweetness that made him Granada's most beloved artist. Look at the stillness: no drama, just grace. Cano could carve marble, build buildings, and paint heaven, often in the same year.

name: Pedro de Mena
teaser: The Spanish sculptor of bleeding saints — his painted-wood statues of the Magdalene, John the Baptist, and the Sorrowing Virgin are so lifelike that worshippers wept before them. His realism made wood seem like flesh, hair, and tears.

exploreAction.targetName: The Magdalene (Museo Nacional de Escultura, Valladolid) — the eyes
exploreAction.instruction: Walk around the kneeling Magdalene: her skin is painted wax, her hair is real-feeling wood, her eyes are glass and tears. Spanish polychrome sculpture aimed at overwhelming devotion, and Mena was its master. He turned prayer into presence.

name: Juan Martínez Montañés
teaser: The 'god of wood' — the Spanish sculptor whose polychrome Christs and Virgins for Seville's churches are considered the peak of Spanish religious sculpture. Velázquez painted his portrait, a rare honor from the king's painter.

exploreAction.targetName: The Christ of Clemency (Seville Cathedral) — the cross
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the Christ on the cross: alive, suffering, yet composed — carved and painted so the body seems to breathe. Montañés shaped the Andalusian ideal of Christ, and his workshop trained a generation. Velázquez traveled to Seville specifically to paint the sculptor — the only portrait he ever made of an artist.

name: José de Mora
teaser: The Spanish sculptor of exquisite sorrow — his small polychrome Ecce Homo and Dolorosa figures in Granada are among the most moving devotional works in Spanish art. He became a recluse after a family tragedy and carved grief itself.

exploreAction.targetName: The Ecce Homo or Dolorosa (Granada) — the face
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the face of the sorrowing Virgin: real tears, darkened eyes, a mouth about to speak — carved in wood and painted with heartbreaking realism. Mora worked in a frenzy of devotion after his family died, and his saints carry that grief. Suffering, made beautiful on purpose.

name: Antonio Arnao
teaser: The Spanish glass painter of the Renaissance — a stained-glass artist who filled the cathedrals of Seville and Granada with glowing, jewel-like windows. His art let the Andalusian sun become scripture.

exploreAction.targetName: The stained glass of Seville Cathedral — the light
exploreAction.instruction: Look up at the windows: prophets, saints, and scenes of the Passion glowing in blue, gold, and crimson. Arnao was among the few masters of glass in Spain, a craft dominated by northern Europe. He gave the cathedral its fire.

name: Alonso Berruguete
teaser: The Spanish sculptor-painter who made Mannerism blaze — his altarpieces in Valladolid twist bodies like flames, with faces that seem to be mid-scream. He studied in Italy with Michelangelo's circle, then brought the agitation home.

exploreAction.targetName: The altarpiece of St. Benedict (Valladolid Museum) — the bodies
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the figures: elongated, twisted, charged with nervous energy — the saints look like they're in the middle of a vision. Berruguete's wood carvings are painted and gilded to glow. He took the calm of the Renaissance and set it on fire.

name: Juan de Juni
teaser: The French-born sculptor who became the master of the Spanish Baroque in wood — his Holy Burial groups in Valladolid are so dramatic they seem to move. He carved grief with a fury that shocked and converted viewers.

exploreAction.targetName: The Entombment of Christ (Valladolid Museum) — the figures
exploreAction.instruction: Stand before the carved group: Joseph of Arimathea lowers Christ's body while the Marys twist in grief, their robes carved in violent folds. Juni's wood seems to bleed. He was the sculptor of the Passion — every nerve of the story carved into cedar.

name: Francisco Salzillo
teaser: The Murcian sculptor of the rococo Passion — his processional floats for Easter week, with their pastel Christ figures and tearful saints, are among the most beloved religious art in Spain. He turned the Via Crucis into a beautiful, sorrowful dollhouse of faith.

exploreAction.targetName: The Christ of the Flagellation (Murcia) — the processional figures
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the elegance: Salzillo's Christs are pale, pretty, and heartbreaking, their wounds painted with restraint. They're carried through Murcia every Holy Week, adored by crowds. He modernized the Passion for the rococo age — and Murcia has never let him go.

name: Federico de Madrazo
teaser: The court painter of Isabel II of Spain — his portraits of the queen, the aristocracy, and the painterly celebrities of Madrid are elegant, exact, and gently romantic. He ran the Prado Museum and trained his whole family in the arts.

exploreAction.targetName: The portraits of Isabel II or of the artist friends
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how Madrazo poses his sitters: velvet, lace, and perfect skin against dark backgrounds — the Spanish court portrait at its most polished. His portrait of the painter José de Madrazo or of the actress Matilde Díez shows his skill with character. He made royalty look human and humans look royal.

name: Carlos Luis de Ribera
teaser: The Spanish painter of grand history scenes and tender genre work — the son of the neoclassical painter Bernardino de Ribera, he decorated the Congress of Deputies with allegories of Spain's constitution. His work bridges academic history painting and romanticism.

exploreAction.targetName: The frescoes of the Congress of Deputies (Madrid)
exploreAction.instruction: Look up at the ceiling of Spain's parliament: allegories of justice, progress, and the constitution, painted with academic poise. Ribera also painted smaller, warmer genre scenes — children, peasants, and family moments. A painter who could do the state ceiling and the hearth in the same year.

name: Antonio María Esquivel
teaser: The Spanish romantic painter of the divine and the theatrical — his portraits of actors, his nativity scenes, and his monumental 'Portrait of the Poets' group picture of Romantic Madrid's literary circle are beloved documents of the era.

exploreAction.targetName: The Poets of the Romantic Movement (Prado) — the group
exploreAction.instruction: A roomful of Spain's romantic writers — Espronceda, Zorrilla, Larra — arranged like a stage still. Look at the faces: young, intense, doomed. Esquivel painted the generation that invented Spanish romanticism, then watched half of them die young.

name: José Casado del Alisal
teaser: The Spanish history painter of the Bourbon Restoration — his grand canvases of the Surrender of Bailén and the death of the master of Santiago are staged with theatrical seriousness. He was also a celebrated portraitist of the aristocracy.

exploreAction.targetName: The Surrender of Bailén (Prado) — the moment
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the moment of the Spanish victory over Napoleon: the French general surrenders his sword, the Spanish officers receive it with gravity. Casado painted the scene like a stage tableau — every gesture deliberate, every flag symbolic. History as a curtain call.

name: Mariano Fortuny
teaser: The Spanish painter of light and luxury — his Moroccan scenes, his famous painting La Vicaría (the marriage contract), and his tiny, jewel-bright canvases made him the most celebrated Spanish painter of his generation. He died at 36, at the peak.

exploreAction.targetName: La Vicaría (MNAC, Barcelona) — the crowd
exploreAction.instruction: A wedding contract is signed in a sacristy, the bride's family and friends crowding around, light streaming from the windows. Look at the detail — Fortuny painted every ribbon and lace with a loupe-like precision. It became the most reproduced image in Spain; he died two years later.

name: Francisco Pradilla
teaser: The Spanish painter of the great voyages — his Doña Juana la Loca beside the coffin of her husband is a national icon of grief, and his monumental canvases of Columbus's surrender made him the king of Spanish history painting.

exploreAction.targetName: Doña Juana la Loca (Prado) — the stillness
exploreAction.instruction: A queen in black stands by her husband's coffin in a snowy field, her court behind her — painted with a quiet that feels like the whole kingdom holding its breath. Pradilla chose stillness over drama and created the most famous image of madness-as-dignity in Spanish art.

name: José Jiménez Aranda
teaser: The Spanish realist of everyday Seville — his scenes of cafes, waiters, and street life are painted with a photographic honesty that made him a leader of Spanish realism. Velázquez's spirit runs through his quiet observation.

exploreAction.targetName: The café scenes or the Sevillian street scenes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how Aranda paints a waiter, a newspaper reader, a corner of a café — with total respect and total truth. No drama, no moral, just Seville as it was. He said painting was 'a matter of honesty.' His canvases prove the honesty paid.
